inline.s: All dharmas are wrought by mind alone; one thought astray, a thousand roads diverge. Know not the place where no thought has yet arisen, and the sea of suffering stretches without shore.
In the still place where conditions are forgotten, in the hour when thought after thought lets go, the coming from the West held no other meaning: it lies only in knowing it for yourself.
A single drop of the great ocean holds the taste of all a hundred rivers. The nature of dharmas is one from the first; only the deluded see it as many.
Men reckon a hundred years long; I reckon a hundred years short — a dream on the pillow at midnight, while the awakened man has not yet turned his eyes.
A patch of idle ground is mostly overrun by weeds; if you but cut them back in time, that is already the mind that leaves the dust.
Ten Verses Shown to the Assembly (Six-Character Lines)
Kill to the last the thieving heart and all its busy schemes; make of your life a trade that profits nothing. Gather up the endless delusive thoughts, and trade them all for a single lotus flower.
The four elements prop up a standing frame of bone; the inch-square mind is desolate as cold space. Only a thread of breathing, unbroken, remains — a tortoise-hair cord tethering the long wind.
You say a hundred years are like a dream — but who has ever opened both eyes? Though you use up every scheme and device, in the end you are a fool still.
Pity the cool and limpid ground of mind: for no reason greed and anger burst out from it. Like a thunderbolt a fire starts in the heart, and burns away the innocence of your own nature.
The body is a false union of many conditions; the four elements enclose a single emptiness. Its movements you call the true master — yet you know not who is within.

Pitfalls and snares you make yourself; who will bear the forest of knives and the cauldron of fire? You think only of the joy of the present moment — how should you know the long suffering that follows?
Your looks are a bearing beyond the dust; your robe, a lotus rising out of water. Look and see what thing is in your breast, and let no idle thought lightly veil it.
The silkworm spins the cocoon that binds itself; who made the moth singe its wings in the lamp? You thought to seek the light by cleverness, and never knew the pull of karma’s power.
A name is but a borrowed name, not a reality; blame and praise fall on the ear like wind. Hear them called thieving weeds — it is a man cursing empty space.
Swing your arms free in a forest of thorns; draw your body out of the field of right and wrong. What you win is a boundless cool indifference — such a one spares no one at all.
Gāthās, Part Two (Three Hundred and Eight Verses)
Reading the Four Marks Chapter of the Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment in Prison
The Mark of Self

Bells, drums, gongs and cymbals raise unending sound; sound upon sound, day and night, preaches the unborn. Pitiful are the drunk and dreaming who wound their own lives: gazing at one another in a mirror, their tears pour down.
The Mark of Person
Jagged peaks tower like an iron city; the forest of knives and the trees of swords are cold as ice. Who knows that fire breaks out from the iceberg? Burn up the iceberg, and the fire is gone.
The Mark of Beings
The iron gate is shut fast, too far to open; bar upon bar — what misery it is. How strange, those who groan through the long night know not for what they came in here.
The Mark of a Life-Span
A single rod of blood is utterly without mercy; once it touches you, it must cut off birth and death. When the pain reaches the heart and stings the nose, then you know the king’s law is very clear.
Leaving Prison and Passing Through the Market of Chang’an: Four Poems
Chang’an’s wind and moon are the same in every age; along the purple lanes and red dust the road never ends. What calls a man most intimately is a single cock-crow and the bell at the fifth watch.
When the body is like space, all is at ease; not a speck of dust divides ten thousand mountains. Pitiful is the traveler under the clear blue sky, eyes wide open, sighing that the road is hard.
Wild winds and gathered rain come all at once; countless travelers cannot open their eyes. Then of a sudden the rain stops and the clouds scatter — the great void was beyond dust from the very first.
A gandharva city and its phantom horsemen in the air; before the eyes it seems a village in the mist. You must walk straight into the city and look: sound and form were never real at all.
Passing Wu Mountain, at Jingtang Temple Meeting the Chan Monk Mingtong as He Venerated the Avatamsaka Sutra, and Thereby Instructing Him

Wherever you go, mountains and rivers are the original truth; the sutras of the great chiliocosm are a single mote of dust. In an idle hour split it open and lightly hold it out — do not say Mañjuśrī is the wise one.
Passing the Iron Buddha Hermitage: Presented to Zou Erzhan, Supervising Secretary

Green hills above the river, spring unbroken; the stream before the gate is pure, without a grain of dust. Opening the door, suddenly I meet the master of the hermitage: it is exactly the indestructible vajra body.
Instruction to the Novice Zhaoli
For what matter did you leave home at all? To cut off love and take leave of kin is no small thing. If you do not seek liberation in the robe itself, the pine gate turns into an iron-walled prison.
Written on the Wall of East Mountain Temple

East Mountain lies close at hand, green and faint; deep in the woods on a clear day the rain drifts fine. Market and stream blend their sounds together — whatever meets the eye is plainly the upward working.
Seeing Master Da’s Gāthā on the Wall of an Inn at Zhongpan, and Writing One in Response
You came to Caoxi when I did not come; I came to Caoxi when you had gone. Coming and going were never in the mind — who would have guessed we should meet where the road runs narrow?
The Rock of Refuge

For no reason a single thought drew in the rank smell of blood; from that time the body’s burden was no light one. Ten years in the hunter’s thicket where the nets are spread — the stones fill the eyes, and all of them are unborn.
Ordering My Young Disciple Dayi to Read the Laṅkāvatāra Sutra

A jade thread is not easily passed through a golden needle; do not question the blue sky through the bright moon. The mysterious pass is cut off and no news comes — go, and when you meet people, do not idly pass it on.
Inquiring After the Illness of Ding Youwu, Counsellor

Who in the world knows this body within illness? Vimalakīrti sat alone and saw the truth the partial reveals. Let great wisdom pour out its torrent of eloquence — a single silence turns back the spring of ten thousand forms.
Instruction to the Two Attendants Guohong and Futang on Returning to Their Home Mountain

A thousand rivers and mountains — to ask others is vain; a single step beneath your heel is closest of all. Do not let your foot slip over the cliff: though you thrust your head out afterward, you have already lost the truth.

Vast misty waters, how lonely the prospect; why ask everyone you meet whether it is or is not? Turn your head: ten thousand mountains, clear to the bone, and spring still brims across the level plain.
Presented to the Venerable Yinting, Who Requested the Canon and Returns to Yanxiang Temple in Nanxiong

Ever since Neng of the South crossed the ridge, the imperial ink at Caoxi still runs wet. Now once more the jade caskets of scripture arrive — wait and watch the rain and dew fall on this burning wilderness.
Farewell to the Chan Monk Gao, Returning to Cihua

A single leaf floats on a cup of boundless water; through misty floods you labor to find the ford. Go home to your mountain, where life runs full: deep among a hundred flowers the birds sing of spring.
Instruction to Zha Ruding

To wade rivers and climb mountains — that too is splendid; your straw sandals came far from Jingting. Enter the gate, and one smile forgets host and guest — do not say Vimalakīrti never opens his mouth.
Inscribed on the Ascetic Buddha of the Snow Mountains
Ten thousand mountains of ice and snow frozen to the root; body and mind in one piece, cold to the bone. Unless you come alive again within death, how can you ever dry up knowing and feeling?

For no reason he cast away the golden wheel of kingship, and by that very act let doubt arise in all the earth. It is a matter hidden deep in the ninefold heaven, never permitted to be known by outsiders.

Lightly he left Tuṣita and entered the royal palace; one glance back, and thought has no end. He walked into ten thousand mountains of a thousand fathoms of snow, and buried his body where no wind blows from the eight directions.

His mind like ice and frost, his bones like firewood; six years of cold and hunger, his mouth could scarcely open. Who would have thought — suddenly he saw the morning star rise, and was left with a brimming smile on both cheeks.
Reply to Magistrate He of Dingzhai

One phrase covers heaven and earth and is ever new; a thunderbolt from a clear sky sweeps the smoke and dust away. Where the arrow’s point presses there is no turning aside — meeting on a narrow road, they are old friends.

Green lions and white elephants ride through the clouds; gold light and silver radiance issue from the same place. If you ask the true meaning of the unborn, it is wind and rain in the empty hills roaring through the tall pines.
Instruction to the Scholar Ou Yuzhong, Who Teaches the Sutras at Helin
This Way is subtle as a single thread, and is kept whole only by the power of faith. Without one patch of vajra ground, it is hard to make every leaf of bodhi shine.
Farewell to Dharma Master Letian, Returning to Mount Kuang
Mountain hues and lake light open like a single mirror; Mañjuśrī has strayed and fallen in here. Do not let the lion lightly flick its tongue, lest it shake the old preaching seat of former days.
Presented to a Sanskrit Monk Who Came from the West

From the West came a blue-eyed barbarian of a hundred thousand li; crossing the river he once snapped a single reed. Even now his shadow lingers in the stone chamber — ask, then: in a former life, was he or was he not?
Mourning the Monk Benlai

Five years, three times I knocked at the gate of Chan; today I seek my teacher, and he has gone and will not return. It is not the white mallet in the Tuṣita court — most likely he is hearing the Dharma on Mount Wutai.
Farewell to the Chan Monk Ruzheng, Who Has Carved a Sandalwood Image and Returns to Mount Wutai
Fire clouds and a red sun fill the burning wilderness; golden light is held within the ancient way-place. Had Mañjuśrī not appeared in person, who would know that coolness is wherever one stands?

Sandalwood from the ocean shore, a pure dharma-body; boundless marks and excellences hidden in a mote of dust. Clearly split open for all to see — face to face, at the point of the moment, one phrase is new.
Sent to Dharma Master Daqian

Thirty years ago we shared the dharma seat; since we parted, no news has come from that far country. Suddenly I hear you now dwell among a thousand peaks — I think your mind is empty and you smell the wondrous incense.
Instruction to the Keeper of the Caoxi Stupa

A thousand autumns of incense seem as one morning; sons and grandsons keep the vigil all night, so still. Tea and broth are offered as though he were still alive — thus they fail not the year the stone hung at his waist.
Ten Poems Encouraging the Disciples of Caoxi

A thousand monks in harmony, like Vulture Peak; that the great assembly takes refuge here is no small matter. Had you not once received his own charge, how could you pass through the Patriarch’s gate?

The flesh body is still present, just as in life; morning and evening the tea and broth are offered with sincere hearts. Bell and drum plainly preach the Dharma without cease — no need for me to urge you again with a bitter tongue.

Seeds in the field of merit must be planted deep; cause and effect are like standing before a bright mirror stand. You have come to the jewel mountain a thousand times — this time you must not go back empty again.

Toil diligently at your work, do not shrink from labor; remember the stone that hung at his waist in that year. When one breath fails to come, a thousand myriad kalpas pass; if the roots of goodness are unplanted, suffering is not ended.
Do not let your whole life slip by lightly; time like an arrow is truly alarming. I fear only that after the last three inches of breath are gone, when will you again walk to the jewel mountain?
The garden of merit must not be taken lightly; every step beneath your heel must be clear. Do not let your footing slip and drift along with others, lest the blind walk in the night again.
A foot of rafter and a tile are made by many conditions; the fat and marrow of the faithful’s gifts must not be taken lightly. Never covet that stake of donkey dung, idly trading away a pair of eyes.

The fat and blood of faith outweigh Mount Sumeru; a grain of rice or a stick of firewood cannot be cheated. Only look at those wearing fur and bearing horns, repaying old debts in the bitter mire of hell.

Fortunate to be born in the Middle Land and to have left the dust early; your body wears the robe and is far from all six kin. You enjoy the pure blessings of the empty gate — how can you repay the Patriarch’s grace?

If from youth you keep the upward mind, a hair’s tip will grow at last to a thousand fathoms. Only after passing through all the bitterness of ice and frost do you become timber fit to leave the Deng forest.
Instruction to the Caoxi Novices Nengxin, Zhirong, Dayi, Jingxi, Tongwen and Fangjue, Who Copy the Avatamsaka Sutra: Seven Poems

Split a mote of dust and the great sutra comes forth; boundless seas of lands take shape one from another. Pine wind and birdsong speak it out plainly — it waits only for the man himself to listen with care.

Buddha-realms upon Buddha-realms, beyond all measure; a samādhi on the tip of a hair is no common thing. Know that when the hand is raised the whole body appears, and wherever it touches, the light of the ocean-seal shines forth.
Line after line, wild-goose shadows fall through the cold sky; upright or slanting, they simply trust the wind. Do not ask Samantabhadra for wondrous practice — first you must know the master within.

When will the pavilion of Vairocana open? The snapping of the fingers must await Sudhana. Then he suddenly sees within the tower an inexhaustible treasury — Buddha-realms upon Buddha-realms, how wondrous indeed.
East of the City of Blessings he bowed to Mañjuśrī; from afar he sought the good teachers to the ocean’s edge. Fifty-three of them sing a single tune — no need to travel far and wear out the road.
If the ocean waves were ink, they too would run dry; a brush like Sumeru is not hard to lift. To depict the lotus-treasury realm of Vairocana — the very first word, who is permitted to see it?
Paper, ink and written words are never the truth; the true sutra lies wholly in splitting a mote of dust. If you can make every word shine with light — do not say Mañjuśrī is the wise one.
Mourning the Monk Yishan of Wangu Temple
Twenty years ago I asked after your health; when we met it was as though we had just been born. Now I gaze far off at the moon over Zhongtiao — only its clear light still shines upon the bamboo hut.
Sent to Gao, Attendant Gentleman
I remember the day we parted in Chang’an, arm in arm in the snow where the roads divide. Now I am ten thousand li away in the burning wilderness — one thought of coolness, and only you know it.
Presented to Master Yi of Helin

Long have I lingered beneath the bodhi tree, and time and again walked in meditation around it. I think back to the day the tree was planted — I once pressed a handful of earth upon it with my own hand.
Presented to the Physician Yan Xingyuan
On the snow mountain the many herbs grow lush and green; plucked offhand, they are used with skill. You are no common healer of the realm — would you let them lie in waste and blame the spring wind?
Presented to the Old Man of Taihe
In the Vajra Cave we met of old; snow-white hair, loose and unkempt, and a spirit all the bolder. One cup of crystal tea and I am still drunk — dimly I remember the old cowherd.
Farewell to the Attendant Xian, Who Travels to Mount Wutai, with an Inquiry After Dharma Master Kongyin
From afar you go from the burning house into the cool; do not speak of ten thousand li of road as long. If you meet Mañjuśrī, ask him for news: in the cave now, how many Chan groves stand empty?
Passing Faxing Temple and Venerating the Sixth Patriarch Beneath the Bodhi Tree

Beneath the bodhi tree we met of old; a thousand years later I come again, and the spirit is still the same. Bell and drum, incense and smoke, unbroken — why then should his descendants hunt for a mysterious trace?
Farewell to the Chan Monk Liji, Setting Out to Visit the Good Teachers
You carry a bowl of Caoxi water and sprinkle it over the five-flavored Chan of every quarter. Do not say old Hanshan has no dharma to speak — these days it is not worth half a penny.
Farewell to Master Jiong of Ruoxing, Pilgrimaging to Mount Putuo

On White Flower Mountain the waves flow without moving; the full moon in the cold sky is the Great Being’s face. If you would meet him there before the rock, look up in reverence and hear the Universal Gateway answer.
Rejoicing That My Dharma Nephew Xingguang Has Arrived
I remember the year I left home and parted from the Patriarch; you must still have been unborn then. Now, meeting after ten thousand li, one smile traces back a bond from a former life.
Inquiring After the Illness of You Shiyang

Let me ask after this body of illness in Vaiśālī: examine it closely — which of it is real? Only when the last layer of yin is stripped away do you first see the gentle warmth and the spring of the whole earth.
